title: The Library on Two Wheels
focus: Past simple and present perfect for background
paragraphs: Every Saturday at ten, a rusty blue bicycle with a wooden box on the back rolls into a dusty playground in Nairobi. Within minutes, thirty children have gathered around it. The box opens like a window, and inside are sixty paperback books, a folding mat and a small bell.

The project, called Pages on Pedals, was started two years ago by Grace Wanjiru, a twenty-two-year-old teacher-in-training. 'My little brother hated reading,' she says. 'Then I realised he didn't hate reading. He hated the idea of silence, rules and a stern librarian.' So she decided to take books to the children instead of waiting for the children to come to books.

The rules here are simple. Children may borrow one book for a week, and there is no fee, only a promise to tell Grace what they thought of it. There is no punishment for late returns. 'If a book is a month late,' she says, laughing, 'it probably means that someone loved it.' Books that do disappear are replaced by donations, usually from schools and from people who have cleared out their shelves.

Not everything has been easy. Last rainy season, the playground flooded for three weeks, and Grace had to hold the sessions under the roof of a bus shelter, with water dripping onto the pages. Several books were ruined, and she admits she nearly gave up. A local shopkeeper then offered her a corner of his shop, where the books are now stored safely at night in exchange for a few stories read aloud on Sundays.

The results are hard to measure, but teachers have noticed a change. According to one primary school head, the number of pupils who ask to read aloud in class has roughly doubled. Grace is more cautious. 'I can't say it's because of my bicycle,' she says. 'But I can tell you that a boy of nine who never spoke in class recently asked me whether there was a sequel to the book he'd just finished.'

Her next goal is modest: a second bicycle and a volunteer to ride it. She estimates that the whole project costs about four thousand Kenyan shillings a month, mostly for repairs and new covers. 'It's the cheapest library in the city,' she smiles, 'and, I think, the happiest.'

title: Review: The Cartographer's Daughter
paragraphs: Some novels grab you by the collar. Valeria Quispe's The Cartographer's Daughter takes your hand instead and leads you, slowly, into a country that does not exist. The republic of Alta Vera, with its salt mines, floating markets and endless rain, feels so real that I caught myself looking for it on a map.

The heroine, Inés, is sixteen when the book begins. Her father, a respected mapmaker, has been arrested for drawing a border that the government prefers to deny. While he waits for trial, Inés has to finish his final map in secret, using only his notes, a blunt pencil and her own memory of the roads they travelled together. Her only ally is a boy who sells newspapers and cannot read.

It sounds like a thriller, and in part it is. But Quispe is more interested in questions than in a chase. Who decides where a country ends? Can a map be honest? And what happens to a family when the truth is inconvenient? These ideas, which could easily have become heavy, are handled with humour and a warm, patient style. Quispe, a former geography teacher, writes about landscapes with a precision that I envied.

The supporting characters are a delight, especially Tomasa, a retired postwoman who knows every secret in the capital and shares only the ones that suit her. Less successful is the villain, Colonel Barrios, who is so cruel from the first page that he becomes almost a cartoon. A more complicated enemy would have raised the stakes.

The ending will divide readers. Some will find it too hopeful, given everything that has come before; others, like me, will feel that Inés has earned a little light. What matters is that the last map she draws, described in the final chapter, is one of the most moving images I have met in recent fiction.

At nearly four hundred pages, the novel asks for time, and a few chapters in the middle could be shorter. Even so, I recommend it to anyone who enjoys stories that reward careful reading. It would make an excellent choice for a school reading club, and it will certainly give them plenty to argue about.

title: Honey, Bees and a Teenager's Business
focus: Present perfect continuous and reported speech
paragraphs: Andrés Quesada is nineteen and looks after thirty beehives on his family's land in the mountains of Costa Rica. He sells his honey at local markets and to two small cafés. We asked him how a teenager ends up with a business full of bees.
Q: How did you start?

A: My grandfather kept three hives, and when he got ill I took care of them. I was fourteen and terrified of stings. Within a year, I had read every book in the town library about bees, which were only two. After that I bought a second-hand smoker and more boxes with money I had saved from selling mangoes.
Q: Is it profitable?

A: Not much at first. A jar costs about five thousand colones, but I had to pay for equipment, transport and the label design. In the first year I barely covered my costs. This year, for the first time, I have been able to pay my younger sister's school fees, and that makes me prouder than any profit.
Q: What is the biggest challenge?

A: Weather and pesticides. When the neighbouring farm sprays its coffee plants, some of my bees don't return. I have been talking to the owner for months, and last season he agreed to spray in the evening, when the bees are inside. It's not a perfect solution, but it's progress.
Q: Do the bees sting you?

A: Of course! Though less than people think. If you move slowly and stay calm, they mostly ignore you. I've learned that panic is more dangerous than bees. I tell students who visit that the first rule is to breathe.
Q: What would you say to young people who want to start a business?

A: Start small and keep learning. I still make mistakes: last winter I lost a hive because I opened it in the cold. But every mistake taught me something that no teacher could. And find someone who believes in you. For me, it was my grandfather, who still sits in the garden every afternoon and gives me advice I never asked for.

title: In Defence of Boredom
paragraphs: When did you last feel properly bored? Not tired or stressed, but bored, with nothing to do and no phone to rescue you. For most of us, the honest answer is 'I can't remember'. Every spare minute, at a bus stop or in a queue, is now filled by a screen. This is convenient, but it may also be costing us something valuable.

Boredom has a bad reputation. Parents treat it as a problem to be fixed, and teachers often fear it. However, it is worth asking what boredom actually does to a mind. Many writers and scientists have reported that their best ideas arrived while walking, showering or staring out of a window, not while concentrating hard. Without external noise, the brain seems to wander, and wandering is a form of thinking.

I noticed this myself during a long train journey last winter. My phone had died after an hour, and I had left my book in my bag on the luggage rack, three rows away. At first I was irritated. Then, around the second hour, I began to plan a project I had been avoiding for months. By the time we arrived, I had a list of eight steps. It was not magic; it was simply space.

Of course, I am not claiming that boredom is always pleasant, nor that we should throw our phones into the river. Nor is boredom the same as a lack of resources. For a child with no access to books, toys or safe places to play, being bored is not a creative gift. It is a disadvantage. My argument applies to those of us who are surrounded by choices and have forgotten how to choose nothing.

So what can be done? It is the habits, not the technology, that need to change. Try leaving your phone at home during a short walk. Let your child sit in the garden for ten minutes without a tablet. Resist the urge to fill every silence at dinner. The first few minutes will feel uncomfortable, even slightly anxious, but that is exactly the point.
Boredom is, in the end, the doorway to curiosity. If we never let ourselves stand there, we should not be surprised when we stop wondering what is on the other side.

title: The Letter in the Library Book
paragraphs: Aoife found the letter on a wet Tuesday in March, when she had to shelve the returned books at the public library in Dublin where she worked three afternoons a week. It was folded into an old copy of a poetry collection, and the envelope, yellowed with age, had never been opened. On the front, in careful blue handwriting, someone had written: 'For whoever finds this'.

She should have taken it to the librarian. Instead, she sat down on the floor between the shelves and read it. 'If you are reading this,' it began, 'then I hope you are having a better day than I am.' The writer, who signed only as 'M.', described losing a job, a friendship and, worst of all, a sense of direction. 'I'm leaving this poem here for you,' it continued. 'It saved my week. Perhaps it can save yours.'

Aoife read the poem, which was about a bird crossing a harbour in fog, and she felt something loosen in her chest. She had been having her own difficult spring: her exam results hadn't been as good as she'd hoped, and she'd begun to wonder whether she'd chosen the wrong course. For the first time in weeks, she felt that someone understood.

She wanted to thank the writer, but there was no address. The book's records, however, showed that it had been borrowed only four times in twenty years, and the last borrower, a man named Mícheál, had returned it the previous winter. On an impulse, Aoife wrote a reply of her own and decided to slip it back into the same book, inside a fresh envelope. 'To M.,' she wrote. 'It worked. Thank you.'

Three weeks later, a new envelope was waiting between the same pages. The handwriting was the same careful blue. It contained a short note and a ticket worth eight euros for a poetry evening in a small café two streets from the library. 'You don't have to come,' it said. 'But I'd like to meet the person who answered.'

Aoife read the ticket seven times that week. On the evening itself, she stood outside the café for ten minutes, listening to the muffled applause, with her hand on the door. Then she went in. Whoever M. was, she thought, a person who hides a poem in a library has already told you a good deal about themselves.

title: Phones in the Classroom: Survey Findings
paragraphs: ## Introduction

This report summarises the results of a survey on mobile phone use during lessons at Unidad Educativa Los Andes in Quito, Ecuador. The survey, which was designed by the Year 11 statistics group, was answered by 180 students aged fourteen to eighteen, out of a total of 420 in the school. Respondents completed it anonymously during tutoring hour.
## Findings

Almost two thirds of respondents (64 per cent) admitted that they check their phone at least once during a typical lesson. Of these, the majority said they did so to read messages, whereas only a minority said they use them to look up something related to the class. Students in the older years were more likely to use their phones than younger ones, a result that surprised the group.

Opinions about a ban were divided. Forty-one per cent were in favour of a total ban, 37 per cent preferred 'phones in bags unless the teacher says otherwise', and 22 per cent wanted no restrictions. Several students noted that they use their phones to translate words and to calculate, and fear that a total ban would remove useful tools.

Teachers' views were collected through short interviews with six staff members. Five said that phones reduce concentration, but all six agreed that any rules would work only if students helped to create them.
## Discussion

The results suggest that most students are aware that phones are a distraction, yet many find it hard to resist. It should be noted, however, that the sample covers fewer than half of the school, and self-reported data may underestimate real use, since some respondents might not have wanted to appear careless.
## Recommendations

It is therefore recommended that the school trial a 'phones in bags' policy for one term, with exceptions for dictionary use, and that the policy be agreed with a student committee. Parents should also be informed in advance, because many contact their children during the school day. A second survey at the end of the trial would show whether the change has had any effect. The cost would be minimal: only about 120 dollars for a hanging storage pouch in each classroom.

title: A Letter Asking for a Refund
paragraphs: Dear Ms Techera,

I am writing to request a refund for two tickets (order number 48215) for the concert by the band Costa Brava, which was due to take place at the Auditorio Sur in Montevideo on 14 March. The event had been advertised as the final date of the band's regional tour. I purchased the tickets on 2 February for a total of 3,600 pesos uruguayos, including a booking fee of 270 pesos.

On 10 March, I received an email saying that the concert had been postponed 'until further notice' because of a technical problem with the stage. The email stated that tickets would remain valid for the new date. However, no date has been announced, and six weeks later your website still gives no information. Since I will be studying abroad from July, I will not be able to attend in any case.

According to your terms and conditions, customers are entitled to a refund if an event is postponed and no new date is confirmed within thirty days. I therefore believe that I am entitled to my money back. I would be grateful if you could return the full amount to the credit card used for the purchase.

I have tried twice to resolve this by telephone, but the line was always busy, and my two emails to the customer service address have received only an automatic reply. This has caused additional inconvenience, since a friend had bought a bus ticket from Salto, which cost her 1,200 pesos. I find this lack of communication disappointing, particularly because I have bought tickets from your company for several years.

Should I not receive a response within ten working days, I will have no alternative but to ask my bank to cancel the payment and to contact the consumer protection office. I would, however, much prefer to settle this matter amicably.
I enclose a copy of my booking confirmation. Thank you in advance for your prompt attention.
Yours sincerely,
Federico Lamas

title: Free Buses for Students, Please
paragraphs: Every morning, Valentina, a seventeen-year-old from Villa El Salvador in Lima, travels almost two hours to reach her school. Two buses and a combi cost her about six soles each day, which is roughly the price of her lunch. She told me that she sometimes has to skip lunch to save money. 'I'm used to it,' she says with a shrug, 'but being used to something doesn't make it fair.' That is why I believe public transport should be free for all students.

The idea sounds expensive, and the main objection is predictable: who is going to pay? Critics say the money would be better spent on schools, books or teachers. Yet this argument assumes that these are separate issues. A student who cannot reach the classroom on time, or who arrives exhausted, learns very little from any book or teacher.

Consider also the benefits that are less visible. Free travel would let families spend more on food and school materials. It would encourage teenagers to use buses instead of asking for lifts in private cars, reducing traffic at school gates. And it would help young people become used to public transport, a habit that many will keep for life.

Admittedly, a scheme like this would need careful design. Without extra buses, existing routes would become even more crowded, and the benefits would be lost. Governments would also have to prevent fraud, perhaps by linking passes to school enrolment. These are real problems, but they are technical ones, and technical problems can be solved when there is a will to solve them.
Some cities have already tried similar schemes with encouraging results, though the details vary from place to place, and it would be unwise to copy any one of them blindly.

Education is often described as a right. If that is true, then the road to the classroom is part of that right. Asking a girl to choose between lunch and a bus fare is not a sign of a healthy system. For a country that wants more of its young people to finish school, a free bus pass might be one of the cheapest investments available.

title: The Village That Built Its Own Phone Network
paragraphs: For decades, the people of a mountain village in southern Oaxaca had to climb a hill behind the church if they wanted to make a call. Even there, the signal came and went like the weather. Today, the whole village of about eight hundred people has coverage, thanks to a mobile network that its own residents built, own and run.

The idea came from Rosalba Cruz, a primary school teacher who got tired of losing contact with her sister, who works in Mexico City. 'Big companies never came,' she explains. 'We were too few and too far away to be profitable.' With help from a small group of engineers, the villagers installed a tiny antenna on the roof of the community hall, powered by solar panels.

How does it work? Residents pay a fee of about thirty pesos a month, which covers maintenance and the electricity bill. Calls and messages between neighbours are free, and calling someone outside the village costs only a few pesos a minute. A committee elected every year decides how the money is spent, and its accounts are read aloud at the village assembly so that everyone can check them.

The effects have been practical as well as emotional. A farmer can now phone the buyer of his coffee before carrying a sack of beans to the nearest town, and a nurse at the village clinic can call a doctor when she is unsure about a treatment. Last year, when a landslide blocked the road for four days, the network was the only way to ask for supplies.

Not everyone is delighted, however. One elder worries that teenagers will spend their evenings looking at screens instead of joining the traditional festivals. 'I understand him,' Rosalba admits. 'But the same phones let our children record the songs of their grandparents.' The committee has even created a project in which young people collect these recordings and store them on a local server.

Visitors from other communities now arrive regularly to learn from the experience. Rosalba welcomes them with coffee and a clear warning: 'This is not magic. It is a lot of meetings.' She says that the technology was the easy part. The difficult task was agreeing to work together, and that, she says, is something no company can sell.

questions.q: Everyone in the village is delighted with the network.
questions.explain_es: Dice: 'Not everyone is delighted'; un anciano teme que los jóvenes pasen las tardes frente a pantallas.

questions.q: What can we infer about large phone companies in the area?
options: They saw the village as not profitable enough
They asked the villagers for a monthly fee
They helped the villagers to build the antenna
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: Rosalba dice 'Big companies never came. We were too few and too far away to be profitable'.

questions.q: Why does Rosalba say 'This is not magic. It is a lot of meetings'?
options: To stress that cooperation was the hardest part
To discourage visitors from coming to the village
To show that the new technology is dangerous
questions.explain_es: Propósito: lo dice para subrayar que la tecnología fue lo fácil y que lo difícil fue 'agreeing to work together'.

questions.q: In 'a landslide blocked the road', 'landslide' means…
options: earth falling down a slope
a flood caused by rain
a strong wind in the mountains
questions.explain_es: Un 'landslide' es un deslizamiento de tierra y rocas por una pendiente, que puede bloquear un camino de montaña.
